name: Jade Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage Oakfold, a goat dairy with a hundred and sixty milking goats, about sixty hectares of barley and grass, and a cheese room where we make three soft cheeses. The owners, the Pells, are in their seventies and live in the farmhouse, and I run it with a milker, a cheesemaker and a Saturday girl for the farm shop. My day's milking at six, then the kids' school run, then I'm checking the herd app, turning cheeses and answering shop orders on my phone between jobs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love it when somebody tastes our ash-rind cheese at the market and their face changes. I use AI tools every day, for the shop orders, the herd health records and writing the posts for the farm page, and they save me hours. What wears me out is the money. I'm on a manager's title with a stockperson's wage, and Kofi, my partner, is a self-employed electrician, so some months are great and some months we're scraping coins for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but overhyped, which is what I already think. My herd app flags a goat with a temperature before I'd notice, and that's good. But the cheese still needs my hands and my nose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means more of the same, and I can live with more of the same. I'd keep squeezing small gains out of the tools. The real problem is still that a small dairy doesn't pay well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and try one or two new tools for the shop, maybe an AI that plans stock for the market stalls. I'd push the Pells to let me take a share of the shop profits instead of a pay rise, which they might actually agree to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless, because I like things to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a profit share change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough to have a cushion, finally. Right now if the van needs a clutch, Kofi has to pick up a weekend job. I'd love one year where we're not doing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job you'd never hand over to a tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tasting. Every batch, I taste it at three weeks and decide if it goes to the shop or the pigs down the road. That's my name on it.

S0.say: It's useful but overhyped, which is what I already think. My herd app flags a goat with a temperature early, but the cheese still needs my hands and my nose.
S0.think: It means more of the same, and I can live with that. I'd keep squeezing small gains from the tools, but a small dairy still doesn't pay well.
S0.do: Keeps running the dairy and tries one or two new AI tools for shop stock planning. Asks the owners for a share of farm shop profits instead of a pay rise.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit restless, because she likes things to move.
S0.quote: Every batch, I taste it at three weeks and decide if it goes to the shop or the pigs down the road.
S0.fieldNote: Jade is quick, practical and already uses AI every day without fuss. Her worry in this picture is the small dairy's thin margins, not technology. She knows exactly which part of her work she'd never hand over: tasting the cheese.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms should get on with it and use the tools, because sitting it out won't help. I'd say small producers can do well if they're smart. I'd probably post about the new kit on the farm page, because customers like that sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is good for me. A robot milker for goats would free up a good four hours a day, and I'd put that time into the cheese and the shop, where the money is. I'd want to be the person who sets it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd look at a second-hand robotic milking unit and work out the numbers with the Pells. Kofi could do the wiring, which saves us a lot. I'd push the shop onto online orders with AI handling the routine questions, and I'd start a cheese-making course for visitors on Saturdays for extra money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and actually excited. This is the version where I get to grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the milker, Shona, if a robot comes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard bit. I'd want her moved into the cheese room with us, not let go. She's good with her hands and she's got a kid at the same school as mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got very little saved. Is this risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's risky, yes. But the Pells would be paying for the robot, not us, and the cheese course costs me almost nothing to run. The real risk is standing still.

S1.say: Farms should get on with it and use the tools, because sitting it out won't help. Small producers can do well if they're smart about it.
S1.think: This is good for me. A robot milker would free up about four hours a day for the cheese and the shop where the money is, and I'd want to be the one who sets it up.
S1.do: Works out the numbers on a second-hand robotic milking unit with the owners in the first year, with her partner doing the wiring. Moves the shop online with AI handling routine questions and starts Saturday cheese-making courses for extra income.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, seeing this as a chance to grow.
S1.quote: A robot milker for goats would free up a good four hours a day, and I'd put that time into the cheese and the shop, where the money is.
S1.fieldNote: She leans in eagerly here and sees robots as time to spend on higher-value work. Her concern for the milker who might be displaced came up when asked, and she wants her moved, not let go. She judges risk carefully: the owners pay for the machine, not her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening too fast for small farms, and the government should help them catch up. I'd say people will still want food made by someone they can meet. I'd keep it positive in public, because I'm selling cheese.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be worried about the Pells. They're in their seventies, and if someone offered them good money for the land to run a robot farm, they'd probably sell. Then I'd have no job and no farm, even if I'm the best goat person in the county.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd sit down with the Pells and ask what they'd do if someone came knocking. I'd propose a lease, me renting the cheese room and the goats, so the business is mine. I'd cut all spending at home and push the shop and the courses as hard as I could for cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My head would be racing, but I'd still feel I had moves to make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lou's ten, so I'd tell her Mum's trying to buy part of the farm, which is exciting and a bit scary. Max is six, he'd only care if the goats were staying. I'd tell them they were.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years and almost no savings, how would you fund a lease?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the bank with the shop figures and ask the Pells to take a lower rent in the first year. If that failed, I'd ask Kofi's brother, who's got a bit put by. I'd hate asking, but I would.

S2.say: It's happening too fast for small farms, and the government should help them catch up. People will still want food made by someone they can meet, so I'd keep it positive.
S2.think: I'd be worried the owners would sell. They're in their seventies, and if someone offered good money for a robot farm, I'd have no job and no farm, even as the best goat person in the county.
S2.do: Asks the owners in the first month what they'd do with an offer and proposes leasing the goats and cheese room herself. Cuts household spending, pushes shop sales and courses for cash, and asks the bank and possibly her partner's brother for help funding the lease.
S2.feel: Anxious, with her head racing, but still feeling she has moves to make.
S2.quote: I'd have no job and no farm, even if I'm the best goat person in the county.
S2.fieldNote: Her fear isn't her skills going out of date but the elderly owners selling. Her answer is to try to take over the cheese side, a bold move for someone with almost no savings. She'd keep a positive public line because her shop depends on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for small farms to find their niche, and I'd say it on the farm page. Food with a face on it will matter more, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I could do well, as long as the Pells don't sell under me. I'd have time to build the cheese brand and get the lease sorted. I'd be forty-eight, and the kids would still be in school, so the money still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd get the lease agreed and put the robot milker in. I'd build the online shop and the cheese courses into a proper business, and I'd start saving a bit from that every month. By year three I'd want the cheese to be the main thing and the goats to be partly run by the robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The plan's good, but there's a lot that could go wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to sort the lease properly instead of in a panic. And time to build the brand so that people come for us, not just the cheese.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. Maybe the government for not helping small farms get ready. But this is just the way it's going, and you either move with it or you get flattened.

S3.say: Five years is enough for small farms to find their niche, and food with a face on it will matter more, not less.
S3.think: I could do well, as long as the owners don't sell under me. I'd have time to build the brand and sort the lease, but at 48 with kids in school, the money still matters.
S3.do: Agrees the lease and installs a robot milker in the first year. Builds the online shop and cheese courses into a proper business, saves monthly from it and aims for cheese to be the main business by year three.
S3.feel: Uneasy, because the plan is good but much could still go wrong.
S3.quote: This is just the way it's going, and you either move with it or you get flattened.
S3.fieldNote: With five years her plan becomes orderly: lease, robot milker, brand. She doesn't blame anyone strongly, consistent with her centrist pragmatism. The risk she keeps naming is the owners selling, not her ability to adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time, and farms that plan now will be fine. I'd tell other small producers to start with one tool and grow from there. That's what I'd post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be pretty calm. Ten years gives me time to own part of the business and build up savings. Even if robots make cheese, people will want to meet the person behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sort the lease with the Pells, put in the robot milker, and build the cheese business slowly. I'd want a proper pension pot started by year five. And I'd teach the courses so that some of the money comes from people, not just the product.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if robot cheese is just as good as yours by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd sell the story, the farm visit, the goats with names. People pay for that already. If that stops working too, I'll think of something else. I always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got very little saved now. Does that worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, but ten years is a long time to fix it. Two years ago we had nothing. Now we've got almost nothing, and that's progress.

S4.say: Ten years is loads of time, and farms that plan now will be fine. I'd tell other small producers to start with one tool and grow from there.
S4.think: I'd be pretty calm, because ten years gives me time to own part of the business and build savings. Even if robots make cheese, people will want to meet the person behind it.
S4.do: Agrees a lease with the owners, installs the robot milker and grows the cheese business slowly. Starts a proper pension pot by year five and keeps teaching courses so some income comes from people rather than product.
S4.quote: Two years ago we had nothing. Now we've got almost nothing, and that's progress.
S4.fieldNote: She's at ease with a decade's warning and treats it as a business plan. Her answer to robots matching her cheese is to sell the experience, and she trusts herself to adapt again. Her joke about savings shows both humour and how thin her cushion still is.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of the Pells. If they sold in a hurry I'd lose everything I've built. What would help is a way for people like me to buy into or lease the farms we run, with some help from a bank or the government, before an investor snaps them up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about the customers. All of this depends on whether people still care where their food comes from. I think they do, but I'd love to be sure.

headlineQuote: Even if robots make cheese, people will want to meet the person behind it.
portrait: Jade Dubois is a 43-year-old manager of a goat dairy and cheese room owned by an elderly couple, who uses AI every day for the herd, the shop and the farm page. Money is tight, with a manager's title on a stockperson's wage and a self-employed partner. She's calm in the hype and steady pictures, seeing robot milkers as time freed for cheese and courses. Her worry in the fast AGI picture is the owners selling to an investor, so she'd try to lease the business herself, and with more warning she plans a brand built on people meeting the person behind the food.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because the elderly owners might sell in a hurry and she'd lose everything she's built.
whatWouldHelp: A way for farm managers to buy into or lease the farms they run, with bank or government help, before investors buy them.
